extracted.intended_audience: NLP researchers and practitioners working on automated patent drafting and patent attorneys involved in evaluating machine-generated patent disclosures
extracted.subtask_description: An expert-informed evaluation protocol and set of automatic metrics for assessing full patent specifications generated by language models, including human annotation categories and embedding-/n-gram-based automatic measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language style
rubrics_metrics.description: Language style evaluates how closely the language and word choice of the specification matches the style a human would use when writing a description of an invention. The disclosure should be dry and factual, avoiding excessive promotional or advocating language. It should not directly reference the claims (for example, by saying “as given in claim 1”) and should avoid "patent profanity," which are overly specific words like "crucial" or "critical" when describing the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scored 1–5. 1 = pervasive issues (excessive advocacy, patent profanity, frequent claim references). 3 = mix of inappropriate and acceptable language with substantial portions in suitable legal tone. 5 = almost entirely in proper style: dry, factual, minimal issues. Minimal advocating language is acceptable. Avoid direct claim references and avoid words that unnecessarily limit scope (e.g., "crucial", "critical"). Also format disclosure as paragraphs (no markdown headers/lists) since patent disclosure should be a series of paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Elaboration assesses how well the specification expands on the content of the claims. Good disclosure should not simply repeat the claim language but should explain and elaborate on the key technical concepts contained in the claims to help the reader better understand the scope of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scored 1–5. 1 = specification simply restates the claims with little or no additional detail. 3 = some elaboration present but much of the disclosure closely mirrors claim content. 5 = thorough elaboration on all key technical concepts needed to adequately understand the invention. Retrieval/external-context steps are important to encourage elaboration rather than rote repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity score
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity score evaluates the diversity of language and content in the disclosure. Good specification should not repeat the same content or unnecessarily extend its length by restating the same points. It should also avoid repeating long strings of text and should use some variation in language throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scored 1–5. 1 = high repetition with substantial duplication or long identical strings. 3 = moderate repetition with adequate variation in many portions. 5 = little to no unnecessary repetition, resembling a human writing style. Automatic n-gram diversity is used (see N-gram Diversity metric); the paper reports absolute difference in average n-gram diversity between generated and original specifications as 'Diversity Difference'—smaller difference is better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual accuracy evaluates how accurate the content in the disclosure is. All of the content should be factual without hallucinations. The disclosure should also not contain any references to nonexistent figures, claims, other sections not present in the patent specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scored 1–5. 1 = frequent inaccuracies including false/misleading statements and references to nonexistent elements. 3 = occasional issues but majority accurate and consistent with claims. 5 = entirely accurate with no hallucinated content or invalid references. Particular failure modes to watch for: hallucinated figures, incorrect mapping of technical concepts (e.g., mixing domain senses), and including irrelevant retrieved information that misstates invention context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage of claims evaluates whether or not there is any content missing in the disclosure. All of the claims should be addressed in the disclosure without any important information omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scored 1–5. 1 = specification covers few or none of the claims with significant omissions. 3 = partial coverage (approximately half of claim content addressed). 5 = fully incorporates all information from the claims with no important elements missing. Assess whether every claim element is discussed/explained in the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-category 1–5 annotation scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural evaluation framework: disclosures are assessed across five categories (Language style, Elaboration, Diversity, Factual accuracy, Coverage of claims), each rated on a scale from one to five.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators should apply the provided definitions and example anchors (1 = poor, 3 = mixed/partial, 5 = excellent) consistently across documents. Use expert judgement to interpret borderline cases; annotators in the study were patent attorneys and inter-annotator agreement metrics (Kendall's Tau, weighted Cohen's kappa) were used to quantify consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic similarity (PatentSBERTa & BERT for Patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatic semantic similarity measures computed by embedding the original (gold) and generated disclosures using models trained on patent text (PatentSBERTa, BERT for Patents) and computing cosine similarity between embeddings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher similarity is better (↑). Because these embedding models have a maximum input length (512 tokens), segment the documents into chunks, compute embeddings for each chunk, and combine via mean pooling to get a document-level embedding. Use cosine similarity between gold and generated document embeddings as the score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent profanity (automatic keyword metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximation of language quality by checking for the presence of problematic patent-specific terms and direct claim references ("patent profanity").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower counts are better (↓). Implement via keyword matching on a curated list provided by patent experts: e.g., "crucial", "critical", "prior art", "necessary aspect", "necessary component". Also detect the literal pattern of the word "claim" followed by an integer to flag direct claim references. Penalize documents with many flagged instances because such terms can unnecessarily limit claim scope or indicate advocating language.

rubrics_metrics.name: N-gram diversity (NGD) and Diversity Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: N-gram diversity is defined as the ratio of unique n-gram counts to all n-gram counts in a document. The paper computes NGD(D)=sum_{n=1}^{10} (# unique n-grams in D) / (# n-grams in D). The study reports the absolute difference in average n-gram diversity between the generated disclosure and the original specification as 'Diversity Difference'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller absolute differences (↓) indicate generated disclosure more closely matches the linguistic variety of the gold document. Patents naturally include repetition, so direct NGD values should be compared to the original specification rather than optimized independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting requirement: paragraph-based disclosure (no markdown)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent disclosure should be formatted as a series of paragraphs; avoid markdown headers, lists, or other non-standard formatting that models sometimes produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating drafts, ensure the output is paragraph-formatted without markdown. Prompting alone may not fully prevent models (e.g., GPT-4o) from generating markdown; check and correct formatting as part of post-processing or as an explicit production criterion.
